body.text: Royal commission says bikie pocketed thousands for fake Big Build invoices
In short:
Bandidos bikie Joel Leavitt has been warned it is an offence not to answer questions at Victoria's Big Build royal commission.
He is accused of forging invoices, including one for $165,000.
Bernard Kearney, from BK Labour Hire, told the inquiry he decided to pay despite Mr Leavitt having not done the work.
Bikie Joel Leavitt has been accused of forging invoices and pocketing hundreds of thousands of dollars for non-existent work on Victorian government building sites.
The Big Build royal commission heard the Bandidos member had issued labour hire company BK Labour an invoice of $165,000.
The invoice was issued by a company of which Mr Leavitt was the sole director, JVL consulting. Two days later, the lump sum was paid into his account.
Mr Leavitt could not recall the exact details of the work he carried out or the duration of the job, but at one stage suggested to the commission it could have been just hours of work.
Commissioner Chris Kourakis highlighted that would have equated to about $20,000 an hour for his services.
"Maybe I would have [charged that]," Mr Leavitt said.
"If a client's willing to pay, why not? Everyone likes money."

The commission indicated it had evidence to suggest the money was a standover tactic and which it suggested could have been for one of two reasons: either Mr Leavitt had information on BK Labour that it would want kept quiet, which he denied; or that he stood over the labour hire company with some sort of explicit or implied violence.
Mr Leavitt sought legal advice before he told the inquiry "to the best of my recollection I've never stood over anyone at BK".
The inquiry later heard from the man who paid the bill, Bernard Kearney of BK Labour Hire.
Chris Kourakis: He didn't do any work for you did he? Bernard Kearney: No. Counsel assisting: Ever saw him in the office? Bernard Kearney: No, I've never seen him, no.
Chris Kourakis: He didn't do any work for you did he?
Counsel assisting: Ever saw him in the office?
Bernard Kearney: No, I've never seen him, no.
Mr Kearney told the inquiry he "decided to pay" the bill and "move on", but failed to explain why.
Bikie accused of being a 'heavy', taking advantage of union power
The inquiry was later shown another invoice for souvlakis for construction workers at the Hurstbridge rail line job, which it also suggested was fraudulent.
The catering bill came in at $9,000 but was inflated to $20,000.
Text messages accompanying the invoice suggested $5,000 was pocketed by two CFMEU health and safety representatives, one of whom was Mr Leavitt.

Mr Leavitt was questioned over text messages that appeared to show a Rebel bikie member asking Mr Leavitt if there were any other Rebels on a particular Big Build project to give someone "a talking to".

Counsel assisting the commission Chris Carr SC put to Mr Leavitt that he was "nothing more than a bikie heavy that the CFMEU wanted on building sites so [he] could intimidate people into doing what the union wanted" and that he "took full advantage of the CFMEU's power to get [his] bikie mates jobs".
Carr: You were prepared to act without morals and you were prepared to be a heavy to get what the union wanted. Isn't that the truth? Leavitt: Not to the best of my recollection.
Carr: You were prepared to act without morals and you were prepared to be a heavy to get what the union wanted. Isn't that the truth?
Leavitt: Not to the best of my recollection.
At one stage, a hungover Mr Leavitt said he had consumed alcohol after the previous day's hearing, which left him "bamboozled".
On another occasion, he invited the commissioner for "a beer" to get to know him better, and revealed using cocaine had helped him complete job-related paperwork.
Evading questions a crime, commissioner warns
During Wednesday's hearing, Mr Kourakis gave Mr Leavitt several stern warnings that it was an offence to fail to answer questions put to him under examination.

"The only reason I'm saying this is to warn you that a finding could be made that you've made what some people would see as outlandish claims of … having no memory over periods of years in an attempt to avoid answering the questions," he said.
Mr Leavitt had responded that he could not recall more than 200 times to questions he was asked during Tuesday's hearing.

He told the inquiry he was seeing a psychologist to help with memory loss, which he attributed to post traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and claimed that during the period of time he was being questioned on, a gang squad had had a contract on his life.
Mr Leavitt said he was also shot, contributing to the trauma, but when asked questions about the shooting, he did not have any recollection of being shot or going to hospital with a gunshot wound.
He also did not remember where it happened but said media reporting suggested he was at a Rebels clubhouse.
"I am doing the best to my ability, commissioner, to get this thing going, I don't know what else to say. It f***ed me up," he said.
Shortly after the shooting, Mr Leavitt said, he patched over to the Bandidos, but told the commission he could not remember why he did that.
After seeking some legal advice, Mr Leavitt's memory appeared to return at times.
Mr Carr accused Mr Levitt of answering questions in a particular way to ensure he would not be caught denying something that might later be proven.
"You persist in claiming that you have no memory about anything that goes to your discredit,"
Mr Carr said.
Mr Leavitt denied doing so.
He was stood down from the commission but advised he could be asked to return for further questioning.
